The evidence clearly supports that high cumulative insulin exposure is a risk factor for atherosclerosis in type 1 diabetes. The study found a positive and significant relationship between cumulative regular insulin dose and carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT), which is a validated measure of atherosclerosis. Specifically, there was an increase of 21 micrometers in CIMT per standard deviation of insulin use, and this relationship remained statistically significant even after adjusting for important confounding factors including gender, age, duration of diabetes, HbA1c, BMI, pulse pressure, physical activity, and carotid lumen diameter. The researchers also found a similar relationship with intermediate-acting insulin, though this association was attenuated after further adjustment. The study design specifically focused on type 1 diabetes patients to minimize the confounding effect of insulin resistance, making the findings more directly attributable to insulin exposure itself.

The evidence clearly supports that inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) affect perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction in asthma. The study compared four groups of asthma patients, dividing them by baseline obstruction status and ICS treatment, and found significant differences in dyspnea perception scores between ICS-treated and ICS-naive patients. Specifically, the VAS (visual analog scale) scores for dyspnea perception were lowest in the obstructed group treated with ICS (group II) and highest in the non-obstructed ICS-naive group (group III). The factor analysis revealed that ICS treatment loaded as a separate factor affecting dyspnea perception, and the post hoc analysis showed different associations between eosinophil counts and dyspnea perception depending on ICS treatment status. These findings demonstrate that ICS treatment modifies how asthma patients perceive dyspnea during methacholine-induced bronchoconstriction.

The evidence does not support that global management at the same centre improves results for colorectal cancer with synchronous liver metastases. While global management (GM) showed some operational advantages like fewer total procedures (1.6 vs. 2.3) and more frequent simultaneous liver resection during colorectal surgery, the key outcome measures did not favor GM over separate management (SM). Overall survival rates were actually numerically higher for SM patients at both 3 years (67% vs. 51%) and 5 years (35% vs. 31%), though not statistically significant. Most importantly, disease-free survival at 5 years was significantly higher in SM patients (14% vs. 11%, P = 0.009), indicating better long-term outcomes with separate management. The mortality rates were comparable between groups, so global management did not demonstrate superior clinical results despite potential logistical benefits.
